learn.title: How Solar PV Panels Generate Electricity
learn.intro: Solar photovoltaic (PV) panels are key to transitioning away from fossil fuels. By converting sunlight directly into electricity using the photoelectric effect, they power homes, businesses, and grids globally—making clean energy accessible and scalable.
learn.c1_text: A typical silicon solar cell has a positive and negative layer. When photons strike the junction between layers, they create electron-hole pairs. This generates DC power, which is then converted by inverters into AC power for home use.
learn.c3_text: India ranks 3rd globally in solar capacity with over 80 GW installed as of 2023. The National Solar Mission aims for 280 GW by 2030. States like Rajasthan lead with large-scale parks like Bhadla, one of the world’s largest.
learn.stat1: India has 80 GW solar installed capacity (2023)
learn.stat2: Global solar generation grew 25% annually since 2019
learn.stat3: One MW solar plant offsets 150,000 tons CO2 yearly
learn.stat4: Silicon solar cells convert ~15-22% sunlight to electricity
learn.readLabel: Explore at US Dept of Energy

learn.title: Production Linked Incentive for Solar Manufacturing
learn.intro: India's Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme boosts domestic solar manufacturing, reducing import dependency and strengthening energy security. It supports the country's ambitious renewable targets while creating jobs and innovation hubs.
learn.c1_text: The PLI scheme offers financial incentives to manufacturers based on sales volume of goods made in India. For solar, it encourages setting up high-efficiency module production units. This reduces reliance on Chinese imports, currently over 80% of India's solar modules.
learn.c2_text: Under PLI, companies get incentives per watt produced locally. As of 2023, Rs 19,500 crore allocated across 13 approved projects. These will add ~60 GW manufacturing capacity annually, supporting Make in India and self-reliance goals.
learn.c3_text: Launched in 2021, the PLI scheme has attracted firms like Reliance, Adani, and First Solar. With plans to build gigafactories, India could cut module import dependence by 60% by 2026. This accelerates deployment toward 500 GW renewables target by 2030.
learn.stat1: Rs 19,500 crore allocated under solar PLI scheme
learn.stat2: Over 80% of India’s solar imports come from China
learn.stat3: 13 solar manufacturing projects approved under PLI so far
learn.stat4: Target: 60 GW annual solar module manufacturing capacity

learn.title: Building Integrated Photovoltaics - BIPV
learn.intro: Building Integrated Photovoltaics (BIPV) blend solar technology into building materials, turning rooftops and facades into energy generators. This dual-purpose approach saves space, cuts costs, and makes cities smarter and greener.
learn.c1_text: BIPV replaces traditional building materials with solar-enabled ones—like solar roof tiles or transparent solar glass windows. Instead of mounting panels on roofs, the structure itself becomes the generator, saving both material and installation costs.
learn.c2_text: Common BIPV includes solar roofing tiles, façade cladding, skylights, and curtain walls. Tesla’s Solar Roof and Onyx Solar’s transparent panels show how aesthetics meet function. They offer sleek designs while generating clean power in urban settings.
learn.c3_text: India’s Smart Cities Mission promotes BIPV integration. The Indra Gandhi International Airport in Delhi uses BIPV modules. With rising real estate demand, integrating solar into new buildings can meet up to 15% of city-level power needs sustainably and efficiently.
learn.stat1: BIPV market expected to reach $88.8 billion by 2030
learn.stat2: Solar glass can transmit 10-60% of visible light
learn.stat3: Up to 30% energy savings when BIPV replaces conventional materials
learn.stat4: India has 5,000+ smart cities planned with green building codes
learn.readLabel: Explore at US Dept of Energy

learn.title: Renewable Purchase Obligation for DISCOMs
learn.intro: India's Renewable Purchase Obligation (RPO) requires utilities to source a minimum share of power from renewables. It drives investment in clean energy but faces compliance challenges. Understanding RPO is key to tracking India's energy transition progress.
learn.c1_text: RPO sets mandatory targets for DISCOMs to buy renewable energy—currently 175 GW by 2022 and 500 GW by 2030. It ensures grid operators integrate solar, wind, and other renewables. Non-compliance attracts penalties, pushing states to accelerate clean energy adoption.
learn.c2_text: Each state must meet its own RPO quota. However, many lag due to financial stress and infrastructure gaps. In 2022, several states fell short by 10–20%. Waivers and hybrid tariffs help ease compliance while maintaining momentum toward national goals.
learn.c3_title: RPO and India's Clean Energy Push 🇮🇳
learn.c3_text: RPO remains central to India's climate pledge of net-zero emissions by 2070. Amendments now include hydropower and storage under RPO frameworks. Strengthening enforcement could unlock $50 billion in investments and reduce carbon intensity by 45% by 2030.
learn.stat1: India targets 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030
learn.stat2: Current RPO compliance rate is around 80%
learn.stat3: Penalties for RPO shortfall range from Rs 1–5 per unit
learn.stat4: Over 175 GW renewable capacity installed as of 2023

learn.title: Direct Air Carbon Capture Explained
learn.intro: Direct Air Capture (DAC) removes CO₂ straight from ambient air using chemical processes powered often by renewables. While promising for offsetting hard-to-abate sectors, scaling DAC sustainably remains a major technological and economic challenge.
learn.c1_text: DAC systems use fans to pull in air, then chemical filters trap CO₂ molecules. Think of it like a giant synthetic lung. Unlike point-source capture, DAC works anywhere—even where emissions aren’t concentrated, making it ideal for legacy emissions cleanup.
learn.c2_text: DAC needs about 300–500 kWh per ton of CO₂ captured. Running entirely on renewables keeps it carbon-negative. Current cost ranges $600–$1,000/ton, but innovation may drop prices below $150 by 2035 with government backing and scaled deployment.
learn.c3_text: India's IITs collaborate on low-cost sorbents. Startups like Enekhee Life Sciences explore solar-powered DAC prototypes. Government supports CCUS via National Clean Energy Innovation Roadmap. If successful, DAC could help India offset 2 GT CO₂/year by 2070.
learn.stat1: DAC currently costs $600–$1,000 per ton of CO₂ removed
learn.stat2: Global DAC capacity < 0.1 Mt/year as of 2023
learn.stat3: Requires 300–500 kWh of energy per ton of CO₂ captured
learn.stat4: IEA estimates DAC must scale to 40 Mt/year by 2040

learn.title: Hydrogen Colours - Blue vs Green vs Grey
learn.intro: Hydrogen isn’t inherently clean—it depends on how it’s made. Grey, blue, and green denote production methods and environmental impact. Understanding these colors helps identify truly sustainable hydrogen for industry, transport, and future energy systems.
learn.c1_text: Made from natural gas via steam methane reforming without carbon capture. Accounts for over 95% of global H₂ today. Emits 9–12 kg CO₂ per kg H₂. Cheap but dirty—acts like conventional fuel despite being labeled 'clean'.
learn.c2_text: Same process as grey but captures ~60–90% of CO₂ emissions via CCS. Reduces footprint significantly but still leaks some methane during extraction. Seen as bridge fuel until green H₂ scales. Costlier than grey but cleaner option now.
learn.c3_text: Produced via electrolysis using renewable electricity. Zero emissions except water vapor. India’s National Green Hydrogen Mission targets 5 Mton/year by 2030. With falling solar/wind prices, green H₂ could become cheapest by 2030 in sunny regions.
learn.stat1: Grey H₂ emits 9–12 kg CO₂ per kg produced
learn.stat2: Green H₂ accounts for less than 1% of global H₂ output
learn.stat3: India targets 5 million tons/year green H₂ by 2030
